entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Neoclassicism, a profound Western cultural movement spanning approximately 1750 to 1830, marked a deliberate return to the perceived purity, order, and rationality of ancient Greek and Roman art, architecture, literature, and philosophy. Emerging from the intellectual ferment of the Enlightenment and fueled by archaeological discoveries like Pompeii and Herculaneum, it fundamentally reshaped aesthetic sensibilities and civic ideals across Europe and North America, becoming the dominant style that defined an age of revolution and reason. Key proponents included art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann, painters Jacques-Louis David and Angelica Kauffman, and architects Robert Adam and Thomas Jefferson.

This revival manifested across diverse artistic and intellectual domains. In painting, figures like David championed stark, heroic narratives and precise draftsmanship, exemplified by 'The Oath of the Horatii' (1784). Architecture saw a proliferation of classical forms, from the balanced Palladian villas of Britain to the monumental public buildings in Washington D.C., echoing Roman temples and Greek stoas. Sculpture, led by Antonio Canova and Bertel Thorvaldsen, sought the idealized forms and restrained emotion of Hellenistic works. Even music, during the 'Classical Era' (c. 1730–1820), embraced principles of clarity, balance, and formal structure, moving away from the Baroque's complexity towards the elegance of composers like Mozart and Haydn.
